Get an unfinished plastic lower for $80. Get a drill press for $100. Get some drill bits for $20. Follow the instructions and use the provided jig to make the appropriate holes. Buy a lower receiver parts kit for $50. Install the parts. Finished lower complete, and you're probably not on the future-gun-grab list.

Then buy an upper receiver, (completed ones are anywhere from $300 - $$$ousands. Match the milspec/commercial tube and stock assy $30-$70 to the receiver and test fire at the range. If no stoppages due to buffer weight, that work is done. Get magazines anywhere from $10-$40 a piece and test fire for stoppages due to magazines... adjust if necessary.

At ~$590 plus a lot of good learning, you'll have yourself a good rifle that grabbers had no business knowing about in the first place... with the added bonus of being able to tell your loved one you CAN'T sell or pawn it in case you hit hard times.

Win/Win.

The WWSD project found that the plastic lowers that are not designed for plastic to begin with are likely to fail. Plastic has different properties and the lower has to have a different shape. They went with the GWACS plastic lower for that reason. All 80% plastic lowers that I know about are re-implementations of the standard aluminum lower and thus no good.

Milling aluminum lower is not difficult and honestly I do not see a reason to bother with plastic lowers for 80% projects. This may change if the plastic lower vendors develop something that is reliable.

I can't disagree with that. It remains, though, the cheapest way to get a working AR-15 with minimal shop experience. It's not like a lower receiver failure would result in a dangerous situation, either, unlike some "shotgun projects" I've heard about.

Shop time, tool temperature, chip hazards and special fitting tools are more of a thing when processing an aluminum lower.. so the entry-level "gun-grabber-averse" first-time AR-15 owner would still find the plastic lower a more attractive option, all things considered. Probably later moving into more durable materials. After all: You wouldn't dream of dropping your plastic lowered rifle on the ground and then using it again without a thorough check.
